strengths: UNOT addresses a meaningful amortization problem. Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measures, and short Sinkhorn bootstrapping is a useful contribution toward predicting transport solutions across datasets and grid resolutions without target-dataset training.

The reported initialization gains are substantial within the tested setting. Table 1 reduces mean iterations to 1% transport-cost error from 16–80 to 3–7, and Table 2 reports 2.75–3.40× speedups on the 64×64 datasets. Cross-dataset experiments, resolution sweeps, and the marginal-error curves in Figure 14 strengthen this evidence.

Proposition 5 provides a meaningful rationale for bootstrapping: for a fixed positive Gibbs kernel, potential error can be bounded using the Sinkhorn residual. This supports generating inexpensive training targets without solving every training problem to convergence.

The manuscript explains the main pipeline clearly and supplies architecture details, hyperparameters, training resources, and a link to code and model weights. These are valuable foundations for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central generator-universality claim is unsupported for the implemented architecture. Appendix C uses 200 latent dimensions for 8192 outputs and does not enforce the Lipschitz condition required by Theorem 3. Although this mismatch is acknowledged, the conclusion that generator coverage cannot be a bottleneck does not follow. Moreover, Corollary 4 is false as stated: take λ=1/2, G1(z)=ReLU(1+z/2), and G2(z)=ReLU(z/2). Both residual networks have Lipschitz constant zero, but G1(G2(z))≥1, excluding every output in (0,1). This requires substantive correction to the theoretical claims.

The OT formulations are inconsistent in ways that affect interpretation. Equation (1) uses −εKL, whereas its stated dual corresponds to +εKL. Beyond this repairable sign error, Proposition 1 omits marginal factors when relating the KL-dual potentials to Sinkhorn scaling vectors. Algorithm 1 then labels the transport-only quantity ⟨C,Π⟩ as OTε, while Appendix A.7 includes entropy. These quantities have different values and derivatives; in particular, f−p is not generally the gradient of a debiased transport-only cost. The experimental target, potential conventions, and differentiation formulas need reconciliation.

The downstream optimization algorithms contain substantive errors as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to an updated probability vector, which is neither simplex projection nor the usual entropic mirror-descent update. Even at an exact nonuniform barycenter with zero gradient, it changes μ to softmax(μ), so the solution is not a fixed point. Appendix A.4 also omits the derivative of the source self-interaction term in the outer Sinkhorn divergence. Correct formulas and confirmation of the implemented updates are necessary to support the geometry experiments.

The comparisons do not adequately establish state-of-the-art performance or isolate the contribution of the proposed components. Amos et al. (2022), the closest learned initializer, is excluded because of dataset dependence, which does not preclude matched comparisons at fixed resolutions. Gaussian initialization is omitted from runtime comparisons. Controlled ablations against fixed synthetic sampling, direct dual-objective training, and alternative predictor architectures are also missing; the qualitative MLP discussion in Appendix D.2 is insufficient.

Evidence for accurately recovering transport plans and Wasserstein geometry remains largely qualitative. The GeONet superiority claim rests on one displayed digit pair, and barycenter and flow results lack aggregate quantitative errors. Figure 14 establishes improved marginal satisfaction, but does not replace measurements of barycenter objective gaps, plan accuracy, or geodesic error across many examples. Such evaluation should distinguish network approximation error from entropic and discretization effects.

The practical efficiency claim needs qualification. The headline speedups use an oracle 1% transport-cost-error threshold; runtime comparisons at matched marginal-feasibility or duality-gap tolerances would better establish solver accuracy. Table 2 also shows a slowdown on MNIST. The reported 35-hour training cost and acknowledged difficulty extrapolating to larger resolutions make workload and amortization analysis relevant to assessing practical significance.
